title: Optimization Landscape Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Data Science
description: Predict where gradient descent will stop on a cost curve with several valleys, run it from starting points you choose, and compare how often plain descent and momentum reach the global minimum.

learningObjectives: Students will be able to distinguish local minima from the global minimum and compare how the starting point and momentum affect which minimum gradient descent finds.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Predict, run, and compare outcomes across many starting points and two optimizers
keyQuestions: Why can gradient descent not tell a local minimum from the global minimum?
Which starting points on the two valleys curve lead to the local minimum, and what marks the boundary?
How does momentum get the ball past a shallow dip or a flat stretch?
Does momentum help from every start? Find one where it makes no difference.
commonMisconceptions: Gradient descent always finds the best parameters (it stops at the first place the slope is nearly zero, which may be a local minimum).
A slope of zero means a minimum has been reached (on the plateau the slope is zero at a point that is not a minimum).
Momentum guarantees the global minimum (it helps with shallow dips and flat regions, but the outcome still depends on the start).
Every model has local minima to worry about (a convex cost, such as the mean squared error of linear regression, has only one minimum).
assessmentOpportunities: Shown a sketch of a cost curve with three valleys and a marked starting point, students say where plain gradient descent will stop, whether that point is a local or the global minimum, and name one strategy from the chapter that could change the outcome.
